translation:
On the Measure of Defensive Qi Circulation

Defensive qi begins its circulation at dawn in the hand Taiyin channel. It flows along the yang channels through the whole body, completing twenty-five circuits during the day and twenty-five circuits during the night, totaling fifty circuits in one day and night.

During the day, the qi moves through the yang aspects of the body. Starting at dawn, it rises from the foot region, passes through the abdomen, flanks, hands, and up to the crown of the head, then descends by the left side to the feet.

The qi spreads to the ears, proceeding from the front of the ears, branching at the fingers, diverging between the fingers and passing along the sides of the hands, scattering upward. It also branches to the tips of the fingers, then the qi scatters and travels upward by five pathways, branching separately toward the head and eyes, following the circuits of the day.

At the small fingers of the hands and feet, the qi branches and separates, passing through the spaces between the fingers, scattering forward to the area in front of the ears, then traveling through the night circuits—five additional circuits.

The qi then passes from the foot Shaoyin to the kidneys; from the kidneys it moves to the heart; from the heart it moves to the lungs; from the lungs it enters the liver. This is the constant pathway of circulation.

translation:
The liver [qi] flows back into the lungs, and the eight vessels converge. In each interval of time (ke), the qi circulates through the body. During the day the [qi] moves through the body; at night, likewise. In a single day and night there are one hundred measures of breath, and [the qi] circulates through the twenty-eight lodges (lunar mansions), traveling forward, backward, left, and right, making two circuits of twenty-some [rounds].

On the Differing Pathways of Ying (Nutritive) and Wei (Defensive) Qi:
The pathetic qi... the eight vessels all converge. [The qi] circulates through the body during the day; at night the purple qi (i.e., nutritive qi) moves. The strong qi moves as a great river; the remainder flows along fine lines. [Master] Yuan-jian says: it begins at the feet and travels one full circuit...

[The nutritive qi] does not exit outward, [the defensive qi] does not enter inward; [the nutritive qi] circulates within the five viscera and six bowels; the six bowels have no outward circuit. But [each] makes fifty circuits of the body — during the day fifty circuits through the yang [pathways], and during the night fifty circuits through the yin [pathways], completing circuits through the six bowels day and night.

[The Yellow Emperor's Classic says:] The commander of the nutritive [qi] is difficult to generate. The origin of life-qi is called the moving qi between the kidneys. This is the source of life-qi for the five viscera and six bowels.

On the Origin of Life-Qi:
It is the root and foundation. The twelve channel vessels have their root in the breath absorbed by the Triple Burner (San Jiao). This is also called the Sea of Qi, the Cinnabar Field (Dantian), and also Guanyuan, located three cun below the navel.

The Dantian is the source of primordial qi for the twelve channel vessels; it is also called Guanyuan, located three cun below the navel. It is the root of human life. The gate [of vitality] is also called the Triple Burner.

translation:
Qi as the Root of Breathing

The Orthodox Principles further state: At the beginning of a person's life, while still in the womb, the qi silently gathers in the Shanzhong (chest center), all flowing downward. For a person, qi has nothing more primary than breathing. Color enters through breathing, the eyes, the method, and the ears.

The qi of the nose gathers in the Shanzhong. In ancient understanding, when one becomes aware of one's own body, a single qi circulates throughout, connecting with heavenly qi. The hundred and ten [cycles of] heavenly qi are the root; none comes before breathing. It is easy to connect with the one ground root; a single qi opens.

Emerging and entering — this is called the mechanism of opening and closing, through which everything becomes interconnected, rooted in a single flow.

Nasal breathing is [like] Zhang Heng's description: one who cultivates breathing regulates the person. The mechanism lies in the opening and closing, benefiting endlessly. Yi Chuan [Cheng Yi] also said: the grinding between opening and closing is endless; who causes this closing?

In its circulation, the six [breaths] rest in emptiness, emptiness guarded, yang and yin in their hexagram functions, regulating inhalation. The six postures are drawn, and through this the breath contracts and flows.

Heaven above, earth below — yin closes as yang opens; inhalation concentrates spirit and stabilizes the mind. The two lines drawn show: opening is for breathing out, position cycling through endlessly.

Heavenly qi and earthly qi — this is the way. The wondrous ability is fully present within one's own body, from the Upper to the Lower Cinnabar Fields, harmonized. Circulating through the person, yang qi emerges.

People in general share this with heaven and earth, coming and going — the wondrous ability is fully present within one's own body, from above to below, awakening the body throughout.

All this is to be cultivated from here and awaited.

translation:
Method of Embryonic Breathing (Ta식법/ Taixi fa)

The True Explanation states: Upon entering, the breath resides in the channels and passes through the center. Ordinary breathing through the mouth and nose is like the breath of a fetus connected to its mother through the umbilical cord — the mother breathes in and the fetus also breathes; the qi merges at the navel. It is at the navel, above and below, that qi comes and goes. This is what is meant by the "heavenly platform" — where spirit and essence entrust themselves to one another, and life is sustained in connection.

In the beginning of learning, one first regulates the breath. Afterward, one does not let the qi dissipate outward through the chest. Breath entering and leaving should pass through the chest region. After ten initial cycles, one opens the mouth — one breath, one exhale through the nose — but the qi through the chest should be as fine as a hair, going in and out extremely subtly. Through a hundred breaths, a thousand breaths, up to old age, regulating the breath in this way with each exhalation and inhalation growing finer and finer until it moves like a single strand of hair — when one can no longer hear it with the ears, when it can no longer be detected — then one closes off the breath entirely, holding it within. This is of great benefit. Once the breath can be held inside without any movement outward, one practices day after day until one's nature is cultivated and the spirit of the immortal sages is achieved.

It is like an infant in the mother's womb: the qi does not go out through the mouth or nose. This is called internal observation. When one can close the breath so that it does not escape — when the spirit is still and the qi is at rest, when the breath resides entirely within — and when one can draw qi deep inside and seal it: this is called Embryonic Breathing. Embryonic breathing means breathing without breath.

The Supreme One — also named Yi — said: Harmonizing the spirit and honoring the qi of the body: one should lie down properly, close the eyes, shut the qi within the stomach region, lying in a warm bed.

The Formula for Regulating Qi, attributed to the ancestral Emperor Gao: At the half of the twentieth [year of age], properly straighten the body, lie down, close the eyes, seal the qi at the stomach, lying in a warm bed.

Concentrate the mind; do not let it stir into confusion or delusion. After deep practice, within ten days the qi will no longer scatter.

translation:
This is why one who has attained the art can place a swan's feather on the nose and it will not move, can endure summer heat, can complete one hundred breaths without disturbance, is impervious to harmful influences through the ears and eyes, free from all evil.

One who lives to three hundred and sixty years of age is one who has hidden himself away in the true path, among the rarest of people. Therefore, the classics say: one who is skilled at cultivating the body and nurturing life...

Without exception, there is circulating qi that does not cease; through this one attains proper order, and illness does not arise night or day. By regulating breathing, one adjusts the qi forward and backward so that the qi becomes stable and fixed.

Regulate the breathing: lay the four limbs flat, soften the body, with the legs spaced four to five inches apart, hands placed evenly, tapping the teeth, swallowing qi.

Draw the body out flat, feet and legs spaced four to five inches apart, hands stretched out, tapping the teeth, drinking in the qi.

Exhale through the mouth, inhale through the nose into the abdomen, fully extending, drawing back finely with force — this is one cycle of the immortal's method of closing the mouth and drawing in.

If it is overcast, windy, rainy, extremely hot, one should stop at the ears and nose, and the fine qi can reach the thousands of cycles, and then call out the immortal's method of pressing the Gate closed.

Guard this: therefore the "female gate" is named; at death the qi is taken in, but one must reach the Gate closed.

It is not through diligence alone that one achieves the right state; the art lies in the space between, in the subtlety of how the essence is refined, the yin and yang are born, qi grows old...

Sitting, men and women alike, moving in equanimity, following along — the physician records: when one person sits with the adepts in meditation facing the wall, the family sits and closes the gate, listening — all of these are the teachings.

translation:
The Lung Governs Qi

The spirit refines and transforms; this is the way to prevent exhaustion. All the various qi belong to the lung. Commentary says: yin and yang in the lung distribute qi through fourteen channels in yin and yang throughout the lung. When there is excess, the breast-center (tanzhong) becomes the sea of qi; when the visceral qi rises upward there is an imbalance. When there is excess and deficiency of qi mixed together, the stored qi is affected. The clear and turbid qi pass through the two lobes, which are the masters; within the lobes there are two chambers. The Inner Canon (Neijing) says the two lobes govern, and within the lobes there are two. When there is thirst, the stomach qi is insufficient. When respiration is impaired, the pulse becomes faint and floating; there is no strength, the face turns red. With excess, the pulse is faint and diffuse, perspiration flows out abundantly. Zhongjing says: at the cun opening the pulse is faint and floating. The channel text says: when the cun-yin qi pulse is weak and faint, it means the upper burner has cold. When the pulse is cut off, it means the qi pulse is exhausted. Wanting to speak but unable — this is another sign. When deficient, the qi is weak and sparse, on the verge of collapse. When the pulse is fine, the deficiency stirs and is hidden; this is difficult to treat.

Pulse Method

Zhongjing says: when the cun opening pulse is sunken and slow, and the guan position is small, tight, and rapid... The channel text says: when the cun-yin qi pulse is faint and weak, there is cold in the upper burner. When the pulse is cut off, the qi pulse is exhausted. When deficient and weak, the qi is about to collapse. When fine and hidden, it is difficult to treat. The abdominal pain is in the loose region; the foot-cun pulse is bowstring and taut, the qi turns against the current, sunken and slow.

Qi as the Root of All Diseases

Qi is the basis of all diseases. External damage, internal harm, the various feelings — any one of them can cause disease through the qi. Those who have life, those with qi, those with cold, those with internal stagnation of qi and its cessation — all arise from this.

translation:
When Qi becomes idle, it stagnates.

When qi circulates and descends properly, all qi rising upward is because the lung has been injured by fire. When disease-qi encounters fire, it transforms; for example, when acrid and aromatic substances cause an upward surge — this is fire converting into fire, causing illness. Because of this, fire causes the qi to stagnate and return. All diseases arise from dryness and cold, or from damage by heat and dampness. When heat injures qi, or dampness injures qi, the resulting obstruction leads to consumptive weakness. When the qi of the organs and vessels is obstructed, it generates heat internally. Disease enters the organs; when pathogens enter, the qi becomes deficient. Yin and yang qi become obstructed; heat forms and accumulates. The stagnant qi transmits through the vessels; when disease transforms and becomes severe, water fills the channels and collaterals, causing a sensation of fullness. One becomes thin from inability to eat. If this stagnation is not relieved, the qi obstruction worsens and the illness progresses.

The disease arises when there is no proper movement or activity, no sustained effort, no maintenance of regularity. People who are accustomed to ease and pleasure tend not to move enough, so their qi does not circulate. Those of high station frequently overindulge in rich flavors; this also causes qi to stagnate and the body's flow to be disrupted. Common people, too, if they are fond of strong tastes, will find that their qi knots and their circulation is impaired. One will not recover unless the blood and vessels are kept in free-flowing order.

Tangerine Peel Single-Herb Decoction (Jupi Ilmul-tang):
Fresh-drawn water; decocted and taken orally. One liang.
For severe cases, use eight qian of tangerine peel. This is a single-herb formula for qi stagnation.

translation:
Seven Qi (Seven Emotions)

The Seven Qi are: joy, anger, grief, pensiveness, worry, fright, and fear. These may cause illness through cold, heat, or emotional disturbances. If they become pathological, Half-summer (Banxia/半夏) is the primary treatment; when the condition resolves, harmony of qi is achieved. The governing herbs support and regulate the qi, and this is the foundational method. It is also said that when the Seven Qi become knotted in the throat, one cannot swallow them down nor spit them out; phlegm and obstruction alternate in the throat, one hawks at them daily but cannot expel them, they lodge and consolidate, like a membrane, or like a fishbone, or like a plum stone, or like a kernel, blocking the upper throat and grinding in the pharynx.

One should take Seven Qi Decoction. When obstructive and stagnant qi accumulate in the abdomen, hardness and fullness arise, eating becomes difficult, pain flares daily, qi surges up and one feels on the verge of collapse; if this persists for five or six cycles without resolution, it leads to calamity.

translation:
Hyanggul-tang (Fragrant Citrus Decoction)

Preparation: Slice the ingredients; add three slices of ginger and two jujubes, decoct and take with a small amount of salt. [Ingredients include:] middle epigastric [formula components], honey-fried licorice root 5 fen, dry-fried aconite, five slices of ginger, pinellia.

Decoct and take. [Use] two branches, seventeen prepared citrus peels, each one qian and a half.

Decoct and take. Each day one should understand that the hundred diseases arise from qi. When there is anger, qi rises. When there is joy, qi slackens. When there is grief, qi dissipates. When there is fear, qi descends. When there is cold, qi contracts. When there is heat, qi leaks out. When there is brooding thought, qi becomes knotted. The nine qi are each different — what diseases do they produce?

The Nine Qi

Bo [Qi Bo] responds to He [Huang Di]: When one dreams, anger causes qi to rise. When there is free flow, qi is harmonious. When the will reaches upward, if there is scorching, there is no free flow, and qi scatters. Defensive qi being disordered, qi becomes chaotic. When qi is blocked and does not flow smoothly, heat causes qi to return inward, and so qi becomes urgent, and digestion leads to distension.

When qi is dispersed there is no movement; when essence retreats, the upper membrane and the middle burner become blocked and closed, qi becomes chaotic, leaks out, is lost, and runs erratically; therefore qi returns inward, and the middle burner's network of vessels becomes urgent, digestion leads to distension.

Therefore the loss of qi movement responds accordingly; when improperly restrained, great blockage occurs; qi is not dispersed or relaxed; furthermore qi turns adverse; therefore the disease is located in the upper body, in this generation, fright and joy — how marvelous.

The spirit, the bladder, qi, the heart: when opened, qi moves downward; when retreating and cold, it flows upward through the membrane and the middle burner; when blocked, qi becomes chaotic, leaks, is lost, runs erratically; therefore it returns inward; the middle burner network becomes urgent.

The exterior becomes knotted in all parts, qi becomes bound; loss of thought causes the heart to have a place to return; correct qi and perspiration emerge — sigh.

Remaining [qi] is all impeded and does not move, therefore qi becomes knotted; loss of thought causes the heart to have a place to return; correct qi and perspiration emerge — sigh.

Seventh: wind-fright qi. Third. Eighth: cold-anger qi. Fourth: loss. The heart qi — furthermore there is something [that belongs]. Ninth: the spirit dims. First: brooding in the heart. Sixth: the eyes look [inward]; returning the correct qi. Second qi.

Like exhausting goodness — heart qi accumulation and gathering. Sixth: the eyes look [inward]; returning the correct qi. Second.

Combine aromatic medicines, roast, use seven units; if there is no speech, treat as wind-stroke, administer the medicines and disperse swellings, first treat then follow-up.

In general, this condition arises from excessive anger, emotional strain, and violent upset. One must be careful of deficiency of true water. The condition originates in emotional excess.

translation:
Short Breath (Shortness of Qi)

One must understand that when the stomach and intestines are obstructed and phlegm congeals, this is true qi cut off from the intestines and stomach. The middle diaphragm fails to regulate properly, and the river of qi cannot flow — this is the baseline. If one cannot breathe through the intestines and stomach, it is not appropriate.

Regarding the upward flow and the regulation of protective qi: when the reality is that it is not true qi but rather the qi rising upward — as seen in detail in the section on the Gate of转 — when it worsens the condition transforms.

Deficiency of urine qi is necessarily a sign that the short qi has turned downward, resulting in leakage of qi; this is what is meant by "the interior." It manifests as the yang brightness disease of cold damage, with dryness in the stomach — this is the exterior of the stomach.

Regarding true qi: when it is insufficient and cannot move upward, and the breathing is hasty and hurried, the qi rushes upward and becomes shallow — as detailed in the relevant section — when it worsens it transforms. If the qi seems to continue but cannot truly continue, this is already the case.

Those with excess wind and improper reception by the kidneys — the qi rushes forward, and the urine is short. Those with deficiency — one observes through the small urine whether it is short.

To supplement insufficiency of qi: true qi should be harmonized. When qi is insufficient for breathing, the lungs govern it. If there is interior blockage producing these four types of stagnant qi, one observes the small urine which is short.

The pulse in difficult cases is sunken. The kidney pulse at the cun opening is short. When yang qi disperses one observes deficiency of the middle. In urgent cases with no strength, use short [prescriptions with] Poria (Fuling).

translation:
Poria-Cinnamon-Atractylodes-Licorice Decoction

On Deficient Qi: According to the Gangmu, deficient qi refers to a diminished, faint qi — meaning that qi is insufficient to sustain breathing. It also states that internal agitation leads to deficiency of the foot shao-yin kidney qi, and when qi is insufficient, one cannot speak. It further states that deficient qi causes a faint pulse, aching bones, inability to breathe deeply, difficulty speaking, and lung vacuity. The formula uses: five fen of [ingredient], two qian of Poria, Cinnamon twig, White [ingredient].

For deficient qi — also presenting with coughing, phlegm-fluid, shortness of breath, and scanty breath: five fen. The Ling formula states that lung visceral vacuity leads to deficient qi. Deficient qi with insufficient strength to speak indicates lung vacuity. Deficient qi of the shao [yin] involves sea qi and water pathways failing to circulate, with form and qi wasting away.

The Inner Classic says that throughout the entire day this condition persists, kidney vacuity with deficient qi should be treated by raising and supplementing the qi. True Qi Pills are appropriate. For weakness with a scattered, faint pulse and depleted yin.

Regarding the four [ingredients]: Ginseng, Huang [qi], nourishing qi. Elder Yang [Jishi] said: Yang benefits true qi. True Qi Pills for weakness with yin depletion.

For damage to stomach qi: benefit the stomach, and supplement to the level of raising qi. For vacuity and deficient qi, Ginseng Decoction and Huangqi are appropriate. The elderly should receive sea-qi treatment; the pathways should be cleared so that lesser [qi] can be generated. Pulse forms that are scattered and severed.

Internally supplement the stomach. For original qi vacuity and depletion, warm and supplement.

Ginseng Paste — treats vacuity of original qi.

Ginseng Paste

[Preparation method:] Filter out the dregs, add water, decoct and refine until no [raw] qi remains. There are instructions for the amount. Short of breath, scanty speech — take continuously, in divided portions, sending down with the decoction.

Remove the dregs, add water as needed, decoct repeatedly three times, then direct [the liquid] in, and pour it into a separate vessel.

Stir-fry internally, decoct, add water, and refine without raw qi; supplement while simmering with Ophiopogon (Maidong) paired with [ginger].

For qi [deficiency]: non-[specific ingredient], ascending Ginseng treats [conditions of] the eyes; use five or six [units]; there is lung fire — supplement qi using Ophiopogon paired with ginger.

Ginseng: three fen as a guiding herb. If supplementing the upper burner original qi and raising qi, use Cimicifuga (Shengma): one fen, soaked and added.

translation:
One must use a single stream of water to make a concentrated decoction. Boil and take it. Taking ginseng alone yields the formula known as:

独参汤 (Sole Ginseng Decoction)
[For conditions of] rising qi deficiency with fever, headache, and a sensation in the head as if insects are crawling — great and sufficient. Use one qian, harmonize and mix evenly to stabilize.

黄氏汤 (Huang's Decoction)
For treating rising qi deficiency with fever, the hundred vessels stirring and moving, with a crawling sensation as if insects move — great and sufficient. Use five portions, sliced: Schisandra (五味子) two qian, Astragalus and Poria one qian each, harmonized and mixed evenly to stabilize. Return five fen to tonify true qi; reach the grasses one qian each; take this decoction.

四君子汤 (Four Gentlemen Decoction)
This formula of Gu's method reduces dampness. Licorice root and ginseng tonify the stomach and harmonize the spleen; Atractylodes and Poria — do not rush the spleen and stomach; Poria, steamed, tonifies the middle and strengthens the spleen; Atractylodes broadens; it is like nourishing the viscera — day by day it broadens and thickens, benefiting the kidneys. It also guides ginseng downward, so ginseng tonifies the original qi of the lower burner.

人参黄芪汤 (Ginseng and Astragalus Decoction)
Add ginger slices, take on an empty stomach. Decoct in water: three slices, Angelica root, Poria, Licorice (roasted) five fen each, dried tangerine peel; Ginseng two qian, Astragalus (roasted), Atractylodes.

Treats deficiency with scant qi.

Yikki-hwan (Qi-Benefiting Pill)

Qi Pain

[Introduction on qi pain]: Qi pain originates from the accumulation of qi and blood within the membranes and cavities of the body. When qi and blood circulate through the body's membranes and organs, blockages cause stabbing pain. In the upper body this manifests as hernia or abdominal masses. In the early stages, one should dispel the yin-fire and open stagnation, descend accumulations of cold and stagnant fluid, and address lingering debility. For long-standing damage from overeating, it is appropriate to use warming and acrid medicines to open the qi stagnation, and bitter medicines to disperse accumulation. Regulating the central pivot and using tangerine peel, trichosanthes root, and hemp to address heart accumulation — when damage has been longstanding due to overeating, it is appropriate to use acrid-warm medicines to open qi stagnation.

Yikki-hwan formula: [Ingredients include] ginseng (人參) five qian, and five qian each of other ingredients. Grind to an extremely fine powder. Soak in oil, combine with oil cakes, roast, and form into pills the size of a grain of millet. [This formula] treats deficiency of speech and excessive talking due to qi deficiency, benefiting and supplementing the primordial qi.

Cheonggyeok-changsa-hwan (Clearing-the-Diaphragm Atractylodes-Cyperus Pill)

Treats: Forsythia (連翹), Scutellaria (黃芩), each five qian, two liang total. Grind to powder and take in red [liquid].

Jigyul-tang (Bitter Orange and Tangerine Decoction)

[Ingredients:] musk, prepared aconite (炮附子), alisma (澤瀉), and others. [Indicated for] water pain and urgent urination, with tangerine peel. Eight qian of bitter orange (枳殼), huáng [ingredient], small amount, one qian of aconite, half a fang [dose].

[Formula for] qi-moving and aromatic decoctions: tangerine, aromatic herbs, lindera, and pills for flowing qi, dispersing stagnation; taken in three fen doses with Four Gentleman Decoction (四君湯); regulates the five viscera; disperses pain; promotes the smooth flow of qi and reduces swelling.

[Prepared by] drying in the sun, scraping off the outer skin, [selecting] the fat, white, and supple [roots]: [treats] qi deficiency.

Fresh Ginger / Shēng Jiāng (生薑)
[This herb:] the medicine is mild, can move qi, disperses and dissipates yang, disperses qi. According to the Decoction Entries: taken with Fùzǐ (aconite), it governs conditions of the qi aspect of disease; used together with Chén Xiāng (agarwood), [helps] qi so there is nothing it cannot raise or lower.

Cyperus / Xiāng Fùzǐ (香附子)
Below wood, disperses stagnant qi. [For conditions of] the lung and the collaterals, use Chén Xiāng as an assistant. [For] diseases of the qi aspect, [use it] to raise and lower [qi].

依人日神名內經曰天心一者生主在人曰神精明出為火無生。

在人回之名總羅。無所其眷養交龍華者。一身奉之主于日名清地之二神府生。

有在陰形包人日神名回之總於無所其眷養交龍華者。一身奉主于日清地之二神府。

於腎陽形象統於無所其奉養交龍精者主于身奉之日清准之三心之統於外。

也內之形象統於無所形素養交龍精者主于身奉之三心之統統外。

形也肥瘦經曰太血上養神盛其次血養形故神主乎其中統三才心之道統外。

去不形類故不可安謹養壽延。神血氣養形故其神者人之神者不必可知。

人千
translation:
The Spirit (Shen) is the Master of the Whole Body

Spirit (Shen)

[Acupuncture points for lung-related conditions:] Taicang, Feishu (Lung Shu), Bailao, pain below, Guanyuan — moxa one hundred cones; for shortness of breath, moxa Daguan five times; Ruler's Gate, moxa according to the patient's age.

[For conditions related to qi and the stomach:] Dapao, through the intestines and stomach; take Gongsun, take Weishu, take Damen, Daling, Dahe; at Zusanli take two qi; at the intervals, three; at Neiting, through Ge, Zhu, Tianhe, Weng, Taize, four — moxa according to age.

According to the Inner Classic (Neijing): Heaven, Heart — the One gives birth to the lord who resides in a person, called Shen (spirit); it is the brightness of the essential spirit; it manifests outwardly as fire, and from it life arises.

The spirit resides within a person; its name encompasses and governs all, without fixed form or substance. It is nourished by the interaction of essence and vitality. It is that which the whole body serves and reveres. Its clarity and purity are the foundation; it governs the three levels, and the heart unifies and commands outward.

Form and flesh — whether fat or thin — the classics say: blood above nourishes the spirit; when spirit is flourishing, next it nourishes the form through the blood. Therefore the spirit governs within the center, unifying the three powers, while the heart's way commands outward.

If the form does not resemble its proper nature, the spirit becomes restless and cannot settle. One must carefully nourish it, and thereby longevity is extended. The spirit, blood, and qi nourish the form; therefore the spirit of a person — one cannot fully know it through ordinary means.

心藏神

地德萬仙日萬事物明之者神明禁中如虛不涉過徑或守而神明

靜典丁良以心通觀乎也心神九七日六至篤而之萬日印之善也持不皆頃矣納是之

下潤不見不其能長久若明也念一宜盡手心靜可以水先生知然不皆故日矣天心是

不生氣故行能榮長若一明念百宜手心靜可以元提出然故矢知天心是

漿藥怡藏神養天有餘疾病則笑不作此此心不足則法悲也毀云內經曰聖心藏日

脈安脈日含神心虛則悲悲則憂實則笑笑不休體笑也皇甫謐云內經曰

士脈

人身神名如黃鳳凰玉鈐肚形如靈烟其字色青紫心七丹元字錦
translation:
The Five Flavors Generate the Spirit

The flavors enter [the body]. The Inner Classic states: Heaven feeds people with five qi; earth feeds people with five flavors. The five qi enter through the nose and are stored in the lungs, circulating upward to nourish the five viscera and six [bowels], cultivating the five spirits, and manifesting the five qi.

The Heart Stores the Spirit

The flavors enter and the qi harmonizes; [these] are stored in the intestines and stomach. The flavors combine to form [something] that has the five viscera's spirit, which of itself produces and nourishes the five [spirits].

Earthly virtue, the immortals of ten thousand [years], say that all things and all affairs depend on spirit-clarity. The spirit-clarity resides in the center; if it is empty, one must not venture [rashly] into byways, or guard while the spirit-clarity [is maintained].

Stillness and orderliness: [The mind] that is clear and good; the heart comprehends and observes. The spirit in nine and seven days, six [levels], reaching to the utmost depth — from the ten-thousand [things] one can recognize what is good; if one does not stop at all times, one returns to what it is.

[The water of the mind] if kept still and pure, can [be like] the water wherein the master knows, yet none of it is lost; therefore one's mind is at rest.

The medicine of the heart gladdens the stored spirit and nourishes the heavenly [nature]. When there is excess, illness appears and one laughs without stopping. When deficient, one acts sad. Thus this [teaching]: if the heart is insufficient, one turns sorrowful. Huangfu Mi citing the Inner Classic says the same.

The pulse of the gentleman. The pulse record says: when the heart is empty one grieves; grieving leads to worry; when the heart is full one laughs; when one laughs without cease, the laughter [overtakes] the body.

The pulse of the gentleman.

The names of the spirits of the human body: [They resemble] the yellow phoenix, the jade seal; the form of the abdomen resembles a numinous mist. Their emblematic color is azure-purple. The heart has seven [spirits]; the cinnabar field's origin-character is [called] Brocade.

translation:
This page describes the spiritual anatomy of the internal organs according to the classical Daoist-medical tradition as recorded in the Dongui Bogam. It discusses the divine spirits (神, shen) that govern each organ of the body:

The spirit of the body takes the form of a divine figure, nine inches tall, dwelling in the cinnabar field, clothed in brocade. The form of the dragon-spirit is three inches long, adorned with song and radiance, its color bright. The spirit of the spleen and stomach governs the middle; the spirits of the kidneys, lungs, liver, heart, gallbladder, and brain each have their own divine forms and names. The Eight Luminaries (八景) of the left and right sides—the heart spirit, liver spirit, nose spirit, and eye spirit—each have names, and the Yellow Court (黃庭) records them all. There are nine palaces within, where the True Person (真人) smelts and refines; within the skull the furnace blazes. The spirits of the two flanks, the lower Eight Luminaries, the large intestine spirit, the small intestine spirit, the body spirit, and the ear spirit are all described. Altogether seven spirits, eight divine presences, and three spirit-forms reside within; the divine names are numerous, difficult to enumerate in full. The body contains one central pillar, weighty and layered; ten-and-four yin, two wisdoms, eight gods, three spirit-presences—the proxy name is hard to count to its end.

text:
五藏藏七神

心 命主乃能身靈之君萬覺千神萬藏之聽
乃故內經胆藏意日五藏神云藏氣也又精也兩精出靈入魂謂之兩魄心有情忘

典之志是謂佐事也七神隨者神意來謂不移之者輔氣也靈化者記也精不者忘精

志而應謂之兩存也謂之智存也

藏氣絕則神見於外

死矢失也問其神無何人日立士入人前喜日觀書是不食善一日有紫衣思思則我故

也服腎絕鮮則神無守至腰戴以神也色亦得是經常思見兩食如女子故我

脈法

脈則脈沉七情腎服沉脈絕結喜傷肝心則脈驚結愁忿傷脾則脈顒促驚愛則脈結顒動作驚恐作忿則脈證師

則脈沉症惱傷肝則脈沉縮結則脈藏故則見求醫外也此謂腎神常見兩女子故
translation:
The Five Viscera Store the Seven Spirits

The heart is the commander and master; it is what enables the body's spirit to perceive — it is the lord of ten thousand awakenings, of a thousand spirits, of ten thousand stored perceptions. The inner classic speaks of the gallbladder storing intent; the five viscera each store their spirits. It is said that the vital breath governs, and the essence assists. The two essences emerging together form the spirit-soul entering as the hun; together they form the po. When the heart holds feeling without forgetting, this is called the two.

The will corresponds and is called the two existing together; this is called wisdom existing.

When the vital breath of the viscera is cut off, the spirit manifests outwardly.

At death, the spirit loses its hold. One asks about the spirit — when there is nothing, a person stands up like a scholar entering before others. One says joyfully, "I see a book — it is good to eat; one day there are purple-robed figures" — thinking and thinking brings this about.

The kidneys' vital breath being severed means the spirit has nothing to guard; reaching the waist it rides upon the spirit. The complexion also changes — through constant thought one sees two women, hence this arises.

Pulse Methods

When the pulse is sunken, the seven emotions damage the kidneys. A sunken and contracted pulse, a knotted pulse — joy injures the liver and heart, causing a knotted and anxious pulse. Resentment and anger injure the spleen, causing a rapid and promoting pulse. Fear and love cause a knotted and surging pulse, stirring and moving. Fright and anger cause a pulse with these signs.

When the pulse is sunken and disturbed, this injures the liver; sunken and contracted, knotted — the stored pulse thus reveals itself, causing one to seek medicine outwardly. This is called the kidney spirit constantly manifesting as two women.

text:
脈而動悲傷心色則此脈緊。九七情之脈惟氣口自緊已成

兩脈已細分癲癇之死又大日長癲滑大虛脈。大日長癲滑大虛實則可治沉心細狂死

為日逆大堅癲癇之死不治浮洪又大日長癲滑大虛實可治沉心細狂死

駿駝其面。而人恐怖也其脈弱何類師日沈脈形如何類師日

浮白而赤面也色繼乎酒心癲神七情一身君主名憂思悲恐驚酒

神統七情傷為病

也。靈又破魂魄神心慮死而不解則忘自傷失

意破魄則恍惚四肢不舉毛悴色夭精死于秋

動中則傷筋兩脛骨不狂志毛不悴色夭精死于秋

人哀陰動絡所傷筋兩脛骨不狂志毛不悴色夭精死于春鄉曰

神統七情傷為病

也。靈又破魂魄神心意破魄則場志以思愿為攝神七情一者喜怒憂思悲恐驚
translation:
The pulse that moves with grief injures the heart; this pulse is tight. The nine pulses of the seven emotions — only at the qi opening one has already become tight and formed.

The two pulses are already thin; distinguishing the pulse of epilepsy and seizure in death. Again when large, the pulse of prolonged epilepsy is slippery, large, and deficient. When large, the pulse of prolonged epilepsy is slippery, large, and deficient or excess — this can be treated. Sunken, thin, and of a heart in madness leads to death.

When the pulse is counterflow, large, hard — this is epilepsy and seizure leading to death, untreatable. Floating and flooding, again large — prolonged epilepsy with slippery, large, deficient or excess pulse can be treated. Sunken, thin heart in madness leads to death.

The pulse that moves in the middle with fright and palpitation will form knotted, startled, and intermittent beats; the pulse is weak. What does this look like? The master says: sunken and hidden pulse is fright; moving and slippery pulse is phlegm.

Startling and frightening the face of a person causes fear and terror. The pulse is weak. What type? The master says: sunken pulse — what form does it take? The master says:

Floating, white, and red-faced; the color continues as if from wine. The mind in epilepsy — the spirit and the seven emotions — the one body's sovereign: these are named joy, anger, worry, thought, grief, fear, and fright.

The spirit governs the seven emotions; injury becomes disease.

The numen again breaks the hun and po; the spirit, heart, and mind — when thought destroys the po, one becomes dazed and confused, the four limbs cannot be raised, the hair withers and the complexion turns wan, the essence dies in autumn.

When movement is within, it injures the sinews; both lower legs and bones — though not mad in will, the hair does not wither nor the complexion turn wan, the essence dies in autumn.

When a person's grief moves in the yin network channels, it injures the sinews; both lower legs and bones — not mad in will, hair does not wither, complexion not wan, essence dies in spring. The township says:

The spirit governs the seven emotions; injury becomes disease.

The numen again breaks the hun and po; spirit, heart, and mind — destroying the po then causes the will to become directed toward craving, seeking to control the spirit. The seven emotions are: joy, anger, worry, thought, grief, fear, and fright.

translation:
Extreme joy and excessive happiness damage the corporeal soul (po). When the po is damaged, the person becomes manic, their will fails to dwell within them, their skin becomes rough, their hair withers, their complexion becomes deathly pale, and they die in summer.

When scorching heat causes hair to wither, the complexion turns deathly pale and death follows. When joy disperses the qi, the spine bends and aches. When hair withers and the complexion turns deathly pale, death follows. When the essence is overstretched and the back cannot flex and extend, the bones ache. This may cause injury.

Death through joy and pleasure — when the warmth does not resolve and the spine and back cannot extend, the essence is damaged. Those with damaged essence show no fixed symptoms. Those with damaged essence show no fixed symptoms. Further injury to yang and yang vessels leads to qi loss and damage.

When essence is guarded within the yin and qi flows downward from itself, warmth does not resolve, the king shows no fixed symptoms, the qi master shows no fixed symptoms, and those in turmoil cannot be neglected. Anger in the center, if not resolved, causes the qi to scatter and close, leading to loss.

Those who overthink find the flow will not stop; when it stops they cannot free themselves from confusion. Those caught in confusion cannot be neglected — the spirit becomes full then scatters, qi stagnates and does not move. When it peaks, anger arises.

When the lungs are affected, sadness arises. Sadness dissipates the qi. Deep sadness affecting the liver causes the qi to collapse inwardly. With small prolonged worry, the spleen and lung are affected above; the heart's defensive qi no longer circulates, and the connecting vessels cannot be endured.

When the heart's qi is imbalanced, the nourishing qi is disrupted. Short bouts of sorrow and anger cause sudden collapse. With small prolonged worry, the spleen and stomach are damaged, and the lung qi defense no longer flows through the connecting system.

Concentrated congestion in the middle and blocked epigastrium cause the qi to be exhausted. Sadness, anxiety, and anger suddenly collapse the subtle functions. With small prolonged worry, the spleen and stomach are injured, the lung qi defense fails to circulate through the connecting system and cannot be endured.

When resentment and confusion damage the kidneys, the person loses recognition of others, desires to set objects aside, neglects things, and wanders in thought — limbs find no rest, anger and sorrow settle in, and the heart qi lingers in the connecting system and cannot move.

Those harboring good virtue and loyalty cannot gain free passage; they lose appetite, suffer at night, the abdomen bloats while lying down, they find no peace, return repeatedly to rumination, the limbs find no rest, and heart qi lingers in the connecting vessels.

Those who harbor resentment, anger, and transgression against fear and terror — their spirit and vital force dissipate, the will deteriorates, and the essence and spirit are no longer collected and governed.

translation:
Joy (喜)

Directly, the hun-spirit flees; cold invades and warmth is dispersed. Joy and anger, if not in harmony, the essence-spirit becomes unfocused. It is also said: Joy makes the qi flow and the will settled, forming glory. When joy is excessive, cold and heat go to extremes, and excessive joy passes beyond measure.

When joy arises suddenly, the channels are injured, the yang qi becomes fixed. It is also said joy turns to longing, and anger injures the hun-spirit. The qi flows and then joy erupts, bringing laughter that does not cease; the seasons of cold and heat, if excessive, lead to imbalance of joy. The heart is harmonized and the spirit settled, the will is fulfilled and glory is achieved.

When there is joy, the qi is relaxed and the heart and spirit are at ease and harmonious; the will is completed and flourishing comes about.

Anger (怒)

The Inner Classic says: When there is anger, the qi rebels upward. Blood follows upward and there may be vomiting of blood, and abdominal distension. Anger causes the qi to rebel upward. It is also said: When anger is roused, the hun-spirit is injured. The hun being injured means that when there is joy it turns to anger, and when laughter does not cease, anger rises.

When anger arises, the qi rebels upward and blood follows it; venting anger through outbursts, it is said anger injures the gallbladder. The great physician said: Extreme anger causes the qi to rise.

The essence is injured year by year. From youth onward, in the yin and yang, the new and the old, passing through the middle and closing off: when anger arises, heat forms and the liver qi rebels. When anger does not cease and the worthy is not obtained, the hun-spirit cannot extend itself, and so the blood pours out causing vexation, and again anger vents and disperses.

The liver qi becomes stagnant; ordinarily the qi clears, and with the school of Dong Yuan (Li Dongyuan) it is said: anger when excessive becomes severe. The spleen is injured. Thus, wood overcomes the spleen-earth. When the spleen is injured, the seven [emotions cause damage], and with the use of medicinals, one returns to balance and peace, mediating joy against anger, so that anger serves as the assistant to joy. When anger arises, the liver qi rebels; wood overcomes the spleen earth; the spleen being injured, one uses assistants — joy balanced against anger — so that anger becomes tempered.

translation:
The Four Viscera Are All Injured: [Formula] Each three qian, take with plain hot water, with licorice root.

Worry (憂):
Internal worry that does not resolve is called injury to the lungs. In terms of the will, worry becomes anxiety; fullness of intent becomes sorrow. In great cold, the pulse of grief does not cease, and above it does not [resolve]. The numinous qi is called blocked sorrow.

It does not resolve; it is called lung injury. The intent becomes worry, the intention becomes fullness and turns to sorrow. The great cold also means the grief pulse does not cease and break, flowing up and down, the heart does not [rest].

Internal dispersal of qi also halts and stagnates, becoming a matter of the will, and turns to cold. Also stated: Huangfu Mi said that when the qi is biased and multiplied, the will arises and the flank does not [settle].

When thought is sought in the heart, because thinking passes beyond its proper bounds, it reaches the two viscera and causes injury. Also stated: In a state of happiness, because the will thinks and responds, then worry causes injury.

Thought (思):
Internal flowing of spirit that does not stop, with hesitation and slowness, not halting, the will turns to grief. Also said: when the heart is deficient, grief arises; when grief arises again, it is said to be grief.

The internal qi combines with the lungs; the will of the lungs is grief. Also said: when the heart is deficient, grief arises. Again it is said: grief.

Grief (悲):
When sorrow and grief stir, the central qi disperses. When it reaches the lungs, injury occurs. Also said: the main grief is deficiency of the heart, the heart qi combines, and when grief reaches its extreme, it is severed. The numinous [qi] is lost; life produces grief.

See Fright in detail.

Fright (驚):
The qi is internally weak and faint, therefore it becomes fear. Also said: fear. Also said: the essential qi combines into the kidneys, becoming fear. The annotation says: fear arises from deficiency of the heart, reaching the kidneys.

translation:
Fright and Palpitations

The kidney qi is the root of fear. The Spiritual Pivot (Lingshu) says: the vessel of the foot shaoyin — when its qi is not contained, one becomes fearful; fear injures essence; anxiety and worry solidify and restrain the feet; then the liver stores blood above, but blood is insufficient, so there is scorching below; fear tends to affect the liver and kidneys, and when their qi returns, fear results.

It also says: excess produces anger, deficiency produces fear. Fright and fear are similar, yet differ: anger and courage belong to fright, while timidity and self-doubt belong to fear. When one knows the source of the fear, it is fright; when one does not know the source, it is fear. Some people must sleep with a lamp burning through the night — this is extreme fear.

The Inner Canon (Neijing) says: fright causes the heart to stir and gives no peace. Commentary says: when fright moves, the inner channels become unsettled and restless.

Great palpitations are characterized by the heart leaping and jumping. This is called "fear of fright." The Warm the Gallbladder Decoction is used for illness caused by injury to the gallbladder channel due to fright, as transmitted in Zhongjing's Treatise on Cold Damage, which says to use water to nourish.

For great palpitations with restlessness of heart and spirit, cinnabar and water must be used to settle and calm the heart and kidneys — this is the method to subdue fright and open the heart. For palpitations caused by damage, there are formulas using nine ingredients.

For cases of deficiency with phlegm, the spirit must be calmed; cinnabar and water pills are appropriate. Danxi says: where there is phlegm deficiency, the fright and palpitations increase; this is the fixed principle. When they flare up greatly, it is blood deficiency.

Such cases are also due to blood deficiency in the person. Zhongjing says: eating rich food in small amounts but drinking a great deal causes water palpitations — one feels the heart leaping beneath the chest.

translation:
Zhong Chong (Palpitations and Anxiety)

Master Dai says: Zhong Chong refers to a condition of the heart that is restless, stirred up, and unsettled — a state of constant alarm and inability to be at peace. It is as if one is always looking over one's shoulder, or as if something is pressing against the chest.

This condition arises frequently in those whose hearts are agitated by wealth and status, encountering difficulties and finding no peace. The fearful and startled, who are troubled, are similar.

When there is deficiency of yin and yang, the eyes may be wide open, there is susceptibility to startling sounds, and the heart is moved upon encountering danger. This is treated with ginseng and related medicines.

When deficiency is present, accompanied by hypersensitivity, with the eyes wide and the pattern being one of zhong chong — a rising sensation, the heart beats rapidly and irregularly, water fails to control fire, and the heart is deficient while water is insufficient — the person cannot be calm without ginseng.

The condition of zhong chong: the heart cannot be subdued by water; the person is restless and uncentered. When the qi descends and the person reclines upward and the condition arises, this is zhong chong. The heart cannot calm itself through water alone, and ginseng must be used.

Formulas indicated: Maidong (Ophiopogon) decoction combined with Coptis, warming the heart; with added ingredients including bamboo juice and phellodendron; Yirong (Nourishing the Nutritive) concentrate; with pine, betel, and willow; with coptis.

translation:
Forgetfulness (健忘)

[This section discusses the condition of forgetfulness (健忘, geonmang).]

The Yellow Emperor's teachings state that when the intestines and stomach are strong and the will is substantial, one does not easily forget. When internally the kidney meridian is full of blood and essence, memory is clear.

On the other hand, when the blood is deficient and the spirit is weak, and when one's thoughts are scattered and unfocused, the person cannot recall things from beginning to end — this is the condition called forgetfulness (健忘). The person cannot remember what was said or planned, cannot keep track of events, and forgets what happened before and after.

The reason for this condition is that the heart's blood is sparse and thin, so the spirit has no stable dwelling, and thought cannot be sustained. When the heart's blood is depleted and the spirit is unsettled, forgetfulness results.

Treatment: One should nourish the heart and calm the spirit, open the mind and settle the will. Formulas such as Gwimyong-tang (歸呷湯) with additions, Bosimsam-tang (補心湯), and Cheonwang Bosim-dan (天王補心丹) are appropriate. Dosage is taken as pills the size of wutong seeds, with cinnabar water-ground coating, taken with water.

translation:
Epilepsy and Convulsions (Diān Xián)

The Inner Canon (Neijing) states: When Taiyang governs Heaven and cold excess predominates, the disease manifests as palpitations and great agitation of the heart.

This is because cold damages the heart and the pericardium. When fluids descend internally, the stomach is stirred in response. The Chen and Zong pulses become wiry and hollow; this is called summer vacuity. The deficiency is located at the apex beat — it belongs to the lung and heart.

When the left side moves, one must trace back the pulse history; feverish sensation arises. The patient becomes emaciated and each day feels hunger. This condition should be treated with drinking remedies.

When the patient is questioned, they report being greatly startled, after which epileptic seizures began, the essential qi became disordered, and evil qi took residence, causing the child to develop yang-type epilepsy.

Wind agitates the diaphragm, dizziness arises, the heart is unsettled; when qi is disturbed, epilepsy forms. Nourishing treatment with warmth is recommended.

When the pathogen is between the diaphragm and the chest, great dizziness and wind-disease arise; the heart becomes unsettled and epilepsy forms. Nourishing treatment with warmth is recommended.

When a person loses consciousness and cannot recognize people, this is called epilepsy (diān jí). When it becomes severe, the person falls and the limbs convulse.

The condition arises from evil qi, which blocks the channels so that the head collapses; the ears cannot hear and the mouth cannot speak, and the patient falls unconscious.

The five types of childhood convulsive epilepsy are named after animals according to the symptoms: lung epilepsy is called sheep epilepsy; kidney epilepsy is called pig epilepsy; liver epilepsy resembles horse epilepsy; heart epilepsy is called ox epilepsy; and there is also the cattle-rinsing epilepsy.

translation:
Gold Pill (Jin Yi Guo):
Three qian of chicken broth, two fen taken with warm water, four pieces of arsenic, two qian; take as a powder with bamboo sap mixed with sweet dew, one qian of licorice, two fen, mixed with sweet dew.

Chubao Wan (丑寶丸) — Treats epilepsy and mania:
Nine portions of steamed yam juice, dried in the sun, stir-fried with yellow ginger broth, adjusted to taste; seven qian each of stir-fried ingredients; each one qian; includes cattle gallstone (Niuhuang), one liang; starred anise mushroom, each one qian; half a qian of amber; grind into powder; mix with bamboo sap, realgar, gastrodia; roll into pills the size of a mung bean.

Chitouan (鴟頭丸) — Treats epilepsy:
Taken down with peppermint broth, five qian of large yellow; five fen; use one owl's head, burned and preserved; yellow malt, large bean size dose taken with drink; one qian of clove, aquilaria (chenxiang) each; blood mushroom one jiao, each one qian; ground into powder; with pig stomach as coating; turnip pill, each the size of a soybean; taken with drink.

Huohu Dan (活虎丹) — Treats long-standing epilepsy of many years:
Nine claws, moxibustion on two or three points, each five qian; fine epilepsy; blood treated, ground and mixed; use cinnabar, borneol, mint fragrance, each; toad ash, one jiao; earthworm, one strip bent; take gall of one; grind coarsely; take four toad skins, one strip; mix into pills; yellow pills the size of a soybean; taken with drink.

Instructions for use:
First dissolve Mengshi San (礞石散), then take this medicine; this medicine can calm the heart, drive out epilepsy and calm the spirit; the illness will then be cured; see previous entry for further guidance.

translation:
Bat Powder (Bianbufsan)
Take one whole bat, roast it with rice paste until done, grind with cinnabar (three qian) into a powder. Fill [the mixture] in.

Yudan Pills
Nine pills: take pig's heart blood, grind finely, mix with mulberry bark decoction, make into pills the size of soybeans. For epilepsy and seizures, adjust with yellow cinnabar. Take one dose at a time until the condition resolves. Grind white dog's blood finely and wrap [together].

Duanjian Elixir (Seizure-Cutting Elixir)
Treats childhood epilepsy arising from Yang. The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) asked: "When Yang has disease, what causes it?" Boiling pork, ginseng root, burned until charred — when the charring recedes, the remainder is ground fine.

On Madness and Mania (Diankuang)
The Inner Classic states: [Madness] arises from Yang. The Yellow Emperor asked Qi Bo: "When Yang has disease, what causes it?" [Qi Bo] replied: using ginseng and pork, burned until charred — when the charring recedes, the remainder is ground fine.

[On disordered speech, abusive words, and failure to distinguish kin from strangers — the spirit and mind become disordered.] The text continues: the Emperor asked again about Yang brightness (Yangming). The patient eats excessively, becomes angry, loses self-control. Bathing repeatedly in water to wash the Yang and Yin qi. The disease arises from the qi of Yin and Yang becoming unbalanced.

translation:
When the illness is severe, the patient abandons their clothing and runs about, climbs to high places and sings, or goes several days without eating, and is able to climb over walls and onto rooftops. As for discarding clothing: the four limbs are the root of all yang; when heat is excessive in the body, the patient discards clothing and wants to run. As for climbing high and singing: when yang is abundant, the four limbs are full of strength, and with that strength one can climb high. As for not eating: there is a pathogenic influence in the stomach, so the patient does not wish to eat. Raving, cursing, showing no distinction between intimates and strangers, and singing while wandering — these are all signs of excessive yang. Bo said: When excess heat is severe, the patient raises their limbs and runs — this is not simply yang excess. But what of those who run about wearing their clothing? The Master said: One who runs while clothed still has yang; one who runs and strips off clothing has yang in full excess. Running naked in bright daylight is so because Yangming governs the flesh, and when its vessel's blood and qi are abundant, the patient discards clothing and runs.

Observing the condition carefully: difficulty in the channels, excess on bright days, wild speech — these distinguish true madness from demonic illness. Madness that begins with roaming without purpose: this is the true pattern. Also said: reckless movement without regard for propriety or pleasure, constant self-aggrandizement — these are signs of mania. Running in frenzy and frantic agitation distinguish mania from epilepsy. Epilepsy is a seizure disorder; mania is a separate disease. One is light, the other heavy. Self-exaltation is mania; collapse and prostration is epilepsy.

When mania erupts: the patient likes to sing but not to dance; speech is disordered and loses coherence; the body is affected; violent behavior indicates demonic influence or epilepsy; if the patient climbs high and exalts himself, it is mania.

Vital spirit is disturbed; the patient loves to sing and dance; the pulse reflects water and fire imbalance; in severe cases the patient strips off clothing and becomes fully manic.

Excessive yang with vacuous yin: the patient loves to sing but not to dance, runs about in circles, and in severe cases strips clothing, runs, and the illness progresses to full mania.

What is called epilepsy involves wild speech and running; mania-epilepsy means rigid collapse and loss of consciousness. Epilepsy involves what is called sudden prostration and loss of awareness; mania involves the sudden fall. There is a distinction between manic epilepsy and epilepsy alone.

Formulas: Niuhuang Xiexin Tang (Ox Gallstone Heart-Purging Decoction), Chengqi Tang (Qi-Sustaining Decoction) for fire-type manic-epilepsy; for cold-type epilepsy with mania of the heart, use Niule Huangqing Xin Yuan (Yellow Heart-Clearing Pill) and moxibustion on the appropriate points for exuberant fire.

translation:
Fengqingxin Qutan Wan (Pills to Clear the Heart and Dispel Phlegm-Wind): For wind-phlegm confusing the heart and epilepsy, Tiefen San is appropriate.

Cinnabar-based pills are appropriate to open the heart orifices and disperse; nine formulas.

For mania with interior heat, Chensha Ningzhi Wan (Cinnabar Mind-Calming Pills) is appropriate. For patterns of frenzy rushing to the stomach and bladder, use Wuchen Blood-nourishing Heart-clearing decoction to treat overactive mania and epilepsy; Tiefen San is appropriate.

For epilepsy where the patient cannot sleep, Ningzhi Wan is appropriate.

Danggui Chenqi Tang (Angelica Qi-承 Decoction):
For heat obstruction: take Danggui to supplement water and blood. Glycyrrhiza and Platycodon, seven liang, decoct until reduced by half, remove dregs, serve warm. Lead with Mirabilite; each time [take with] Rhubarb, remove from the stomach; Jade [dose] two liang, Mirabilitum.

Huanglian Xiexin Tang (Coptis Heart-Draining Decoction):
Treats phlegm disorders. Rhubarb, Licorice, tea [Pinellia] half, one liang each; Coptis, each five [fen]; lead with Rehmannia water, decocted, each dose one [qian]; Tritici Fructus, large [dose].

Niuhuang Xiexin Tang (Bezoar Heart-Draining Decoction):
Grind the right ingredients into powder. Treats heart conditions. Each time [for] epilepsy, two [liang]; take with fresh ginger juice, extremely [heated], to address heart evil-heat; combine with water-levigated [mineral]; for mania, Bovine Bezoar and Shen [ingredients], each not one [full] Tritici Fructus large dose.

Tiefen San (Iron Powder Powder):
Adjust the right ingredients, ground into powder. Treats heart-below [conditions]. Each dose: drive [out the pathogen]; one qian; fresh ginger, two liang; with southern [ginger] juice, boiled to the extreme, addresses heart evil heat; combine with water-levigated [mineral] for mania; Bovine Bezoar, Shen, each not one Tritici large dose.
[Amounts:] qian, liang, whole Scorpion, large; five; Cinnabar, Arsenolite, Gold foil; thirty pieces; the right ingredients all ground into powder; each dose four qian; Pinellia, [prepared] five [portions]; one southern [ingredient].
Two [liang]: White [ingredient], White [ingredient], Prepared Aconite, Pinellia, Chuanxiong, large southern [ingredient].

translation:
Old formula says: Take four liang of juice, mix and take. If it causes a burning or spicy sensation, add a little warm water to suppress liver pathogenic qi and calm the spirit. This is a special and remarkable method.

The formula says: Anger injures the liver; when the liver is excessively stirred, madness results. Treatment uses iron filings (tie fen) to subdue and suppress it. Iron filings are the correct substance.

The Inner Canon (Nei Jing) says: For yang reversal with mad rage that does not recover, seven factors apply. Use iron shavings (sheng tie luo) as a drink.

Yuijin Pill (Curcuma Pill)

Form into pills. Treats epilepsy and mania with long-standing stagnation that does not improve, in cases involving fright, anxiety, and worry. Iron filings are added. Take three doses. Retained in the chest area.

There is a sensation of something leaving, the spirit and qi clear. Each time take five [pills] with wine. For ten or nine doses, with decoction of heron...iron filings obtained. Retained thinly on the heart.

Tongsie Powder (Purgative Dispersing Powder)

Commander [of the formula] — good for treating stagnation. Settle the three [types of] mania and madness. Add powder or use wind [method]. Right side: violent water action, able to remove heart disease. Adjust, consolidate, continue, then pour [into the mouth].

Take five qian, make into [a mixture], use to frighten and test. At the extreme, the powder is taken by the river side, not too light. Combine with cold, adjust, fix, continue to pour.

Zhenshin Pill (Calming the Heart Pill)

For this: steam and sun-dry until cut thoroughly. Do not allow the patient to be aware. Bitter, on its own one dose — no [water from the] well, just above [ground level]. One [portion] comes out, contained with cinnabar. The heart is suddenly seized by mania, unable to stop. Physician traces: immediately expelled.

People treat white mania and madness with the bitter clove powder formula. No well [water]; in the same manner, from Huabei [northern region], water is wrapped. Suddenly mania follows; when obtained, the great origin vomits true [phlegm], vomits melon stalk.

Dissolve and decoct below, combine half. Now divide cinnabar [proportions], form into powder. If water pills, two liang: benevolence [ren], worry, great [da], chen [pi], arsenic [pi], water-levigated, one [batch of] nine [pills].

Ye Family Xiong-Zhu Pill (Ye Shi Xiong Zhu Jiu)
This treats cases where fright or excessive worry causes loss of mental clarity, or where too much brooding accumulates and develops into epilepsy or mania. Use a decoction to tonify and benefit the heart and gallbladder, to calm and settle the spirit. Separately use cinnabar (zhusha) as a coating; each half-measure forms pellets the size of pig-heart kernels, using pig-heart blood and calamus blood [as binders].

Harmonize and form into pills; take with a decoction to nourish and balance the heart. It treats conditions where depressed qi in the pericardium causes manic speech and running about wildly.

Zui Gao (Intoxicating Paste/Ointment)
For the condition described above: wait until it is cooked, [add] sesame oil or mix as appropriate; if the person vomits upon intake, or if there are symptoms of heart disease, decoct until seven-tenths remain, divide into two portions, and take daily; change the formula according to local conditions.

Pour in [the medicine]; if it cannot be treated by ordinary means, [it works] like a divine remedy — the patient may vomit on intake, or symptoms of madness and epilepsy may develop.

Gua-Sha Ning-Zhi Pill (Melon Seed Cinnabar Mind-Settling Pill)
Cinnabar (Chensha), two liang, prepared; Acorus (Shichangpu); Ziziphus seed (Suanzaoren), stir-fried; place in cloth bags; decoct with rice-washing water; use wine toward the end, until the decoction is almost exhausted; remove the heart diseases; make into pills the size of mung beans; at bedtime, grind and take promptly.

Shi Zhi Hua Tan Tang (Resolve Phlegm and Settle the Will Decoction)
Coptis (Huanglian), stir-fried with ginger juice; Gastrodia (Tianma); prepared Arisaema (Nanxing); Pinellia (Banxia); Tangerine peel (Chenpi); stir-fried Bamboo shavings (Danzhuyu).

Yanghyeol Cheongshim-tang (Blood-Nourishing Heart-Clearing Decoction)

Ingredients: Danggwi (Angelica sinensis) and Saengjiwhang (Rehmannia glutinosa), each 1 qian and a half; Insam (Ginseng), each 1 qian; Baekchul (Atractylodes); Boksin (Poria with hostwood); Sanjoinhyeon (dry-fried sour jujube seed); Cheongung (Ligusticum chuanxiong), each 1 qian; Gamcho (licorice).

Prepare 5 fen. Cut the ingredients into one packet. Add 5 slices of ginger and water and decoct. Take the decoction. Divide on the right. Decoct again and take. Return to raw earth-yellow. Prepare acidified jujube kernel, stir-fried. Chuanxiong, each 1 qian. Ginseng, each 1 qian. White atractylodes, poria, spirit-calming poria.

Ochemyuk (Ox Carriage Meat Decoction)

Treats raving madness, talking to walls, running about. Take both doses of the sour drink. The person who is slightly intoxicated cannot place the illness — the drink trembles.

Jinsha-san (Cinnabar Powder)

Treats bright sores, mania, talking to walls nonsensically, running about wildly in a deranged state. Take two portions of the soul-sour drink; the person who is a guardian should slightly refrain — what should one do? Place the illness — the drink trembles.

Treatment method: Bring the patient to a quiet room. Place him in a bed in a deeply intoxicated state. Calm him and make him comfortable. Grind the medicine to a fine powder. Do not make one dose first — take one liang of the sour drink. The person who guards it should slightly not know where to place the illness. Drink trembles.

Wait until he wakes of his own accord the next day after becoming thoroughly sober. Let his spirit settle. In no way should anyone startle him; also do not allow him to be startled or agitated so as to shock the brain upon waking.

At dawn, having waited one day, when he is fully sober, let his spirit be settled. Under no circumstances whatsoever should he be startled, nor may one again startle or agitate him to shock the brain upon waking from the two-liang treatment.

Someone came down the road in the morning — suddenly afflicted with madness. Every evening at his home he stole wine. The abundance of fruit and such was thereby obtained. But sleeplessness, with all sorts of things attached — the physician adjusted the medicines; the physician Sun, with seven signs, administered the medicine together with it. Wait the day, urinate; now withdraw. Withdrawing now.

translation:
Signs of Spirit Disorders That Cannot Be Treated

The Inner Classic states: those who retain their spirit flourish. The Lingshu says: those with epilepsy are called those who have lost their spirit.

When the mind closes off and the spleen qi becomes knotted, and one cannot eat meals, the condition belongs to the liver wood. If one loses the ability to think clearly, the wood becomes exhausted and madness arises.

[A case:] A woman sat brooding, unable to return home in her thoughts, and the obstruction grew. The woman's condition worsened and she became isolated and difficult to treat. At a certain time, joy could provide some relief and the father sought a physician.

The physician said that to reduce her symptoms, food should be increased monthly. He also had the woman made to laugh, and used cinnabar powder along with a female entertainer dressed up, so that the woman would eat and drink again.

[The treatment principle:] This method of using anger to resolve the condition — only a person of wisdom can apply it. Sadness and brooding are overcome by joy; grief in the lungs is overcome by fear; joy that has caused damage is overcome by sorrow. Worry is resolved by joy; fear is overcome by thought; and that which is harmed by sorrow is resolved by joy, and overcome by fear.

When the vital qi descends and leaks away, the condition is untreatable. Ninth point. For the diseases of mania, epilepsy, and convulsions: when the spirit has departed, the eyes stare blankly and the patient cannot eat.

When there is a condition of confusion and bewilderment, it cannot be treated; it resembles mania leading to death. For spirit-loss type epileptic mania, when the eyes stare blankly and the patient cannot eat normally, it is untreatable.

When the affliction does not flare up, it can be treated through the liver. Mania and epilepsy that cannot be treated are categorized under the liver.

The qi of such persons — the spirit guards over it; blood is the basis; fright leads to fear.

In regulating the emotions: those who dwell in stagnation need to drain the stagnant water; to calm the mind, settle fright and stabilize the spirit.

The mind governs blood; blood nourishes the spirit; settling fright and calming fear address the deficiency.

When there is phlegm-fire causing epilepsy and mania, one should calm the spirit alone.

Treat by using emetic methods to expel upward. Use the Treasure formulas; for long-standing mania and epilepsy that will not resolve, calm the spirit and nourish it.

Use the Three Descending Qi and Fire Decoctions to clear obstruction; for chronic unremitting mania and epilepsy, nourish and calm the spirit.

All arise from yang transforming into fire; the spirit-qi becomes chaotic, and the condition becomes subtler over time; on certain days induce vomiting; for those worn down by overexertion, after extremity of fatigue.

The five emotions and the fire of the five minds: when heart-fire dominates alone, the heart reaches outward in disorder, and the illness becomes mild; after excessive overexertion.

Evidence: the five emotions and the heart-fire as the chief cause. Fire: when one experiences excessive joy, agitation, fright, and fear — these all pertain to yang.

Tianwang Buxin Dan (Heavenly Emperor's Heart-Nourishing Pill)

[Preparation method:] Boil together, dry and suspend in a bag, add white spirit and ginger juice, press and cook. Each day use three portions of calamus. Large portions of cinnabar. Place eighteen pecks of charcoal in a pit, set a basin inside. Cut open and take the meat, put it inside a green bag, burn over good fire with ten catties of wine.

Ingredients include: malt/ophiopogon, two liang each; polygala; taken at bedtime; jade bamboo leaves; ground to powder; stir-fried with wine; Chinese angelica; washed with wine; coptis; washed five times; grain of paradise; universal gate; coptis; stir-fried; nourishing.

Jiwei Ningshen Wan (Modified Spirit-Calming Pill)

[Take] at bedtime. Malt/ophiopogon, two liang each. Polygala. [For] carbuncles and ulcers. Decoct in broth. Stir-fry with honey. Stir-fried Chinese angelica, washed with wine. Five征. Two liang of coptis. Polygala. Nourishing. Stir-fried.

Medicinal ingredients: Ligusticum chuanxiong, bagged; shen; ophiopogon, one liang each; jujube seed; aged tangerine peel; coptis, stir-fried; licorice, five qian each. Grind to powder and cut evenly.

Honey decoction. Poria, seven qian each. Jujube, five large ones. Cinnabar. Polygala. Codonopsis. Ophiopogon. Stir-fried. Nourishing.

Augmented and Reduced Warm Gallbladder Decoction

Treats palpitations, anxiety, fear, and fright; calms the spirit; addresses heart damage from worry.

Ingredients include: bamboo juice (zhuli), pinellia (banxia) with cinnabar, roasted bamboo shavings, poria with spirit (fushen), schisandra (wuweizi), white atractylodes (baizhu), poria (fuling), ophiopogon (maimendong) — each in specified amounts — codonopsis (renshen) 6 fen, anemarrhena (zhimu) 1 qian, magnetite (cishi) powder 1 qian, 5 fen; sour jujube kernel (suanzaoren), polygala (yuanzhi), tangerine peel (chenpi), processed pinellia (zhibanxia) — along with ginger slices, water decoction.

Nourish the Heart Pill

Treats heart deficiency with sweating, palpitations, and fright. Roasted sour jujube kernel, polygala (yuanzhi) — each 2 liang, 1 liang respectively; renshen (codonopsis) and amber (hupo), each 5 qian; chuanxiong 3 qian, acorus (shichangpu), dried rehmannia (gandihuang) — each 6 qian; licorice (gancao) 3 liang, gold foil 50 sheets, cinnabar for coating, mume (wumei) — 2 liang. This is a proven formula.

Single Remedies (3 kinds):

Cinnabar (Zhusha)
This calms the spirit, settles the ethereal and corporeal souls (hun and po), relieves mental unrest. Grind finely, take in water — this is a proven treatment for fright and palpitations. Refine and use. Also said: dissolve in water, one dou, simmer, strain clear, drink in small sips — this likewise treats fright conditions.

Yellow Soybeans
Proven formula: use with large dates (dazao) and cinnabar, 50 qian, gold foil coating, 2 liang. Proven formula cited.

Purple Quartz (Zishiying)
Take 2 sheng, simmer, strain clear, drink in small sips. For those suffering from severe fright — comparable in clarity to rock crystal. Refine and take.

Mercury (Quicksilver)
Opens channels, calms the spirit. Settles the mind, stabilizes the heart. Makes a person store [qi in the] heart. Rectifies [the spirit]. [Cited in] Yangzi's writings. [Used for treating] portal spirit disorders. Cinnabar. Mixed with cinnabar, taken for a long time.

Iron Water (Fermented Iron Liquid)
For nine [doses]: take fire-treated iron. For treating epilepsy and madness — place the iron vessels [with the liquid], let it ferment. For those suffering from mania and epilepsy, soak in water to treat heart [disorders] and [disturbed] qi. For chronic cases of mania where the patient runs about wildly, take [this preparation] when the patient craves drink and pants. Grind finely with red stone [minerals], seal with paste and cinnabar, burn with charcoal, sprinkle with vinegar twice, soak for two nights, then take. Grind the yellow cinnabar finely, add to water.

Minium (Red Lead, Huangdan)
Calms and settles the mind. Tranquilizes and stabilizes. Suppresses [pathological movement]. Stops [palpitations]. In ninety parts, mix wine, stir together, and drink one hundred days' worth. Then day by day, [the patient] will no longer forget things.

Ginseng (Renshen)
Ginseng powder settles the spirit, stabilizes [the mind], suppresses [agitation]. In nine doses [for those who] wander off or have open heart [deficiency], the spirit is collected and used. The spirit [is restored so the patient] no longer forgets.

Asparagus Root (Tianmendong)
Moistens the skin, calms and stabilizes [the mind], suppresses [agitation]. Stops [the discharge of] fluids, strengthens the will, stores [vital essence]. For mania, take [it] and refine the heart into fine powder. [Taken] internally and externally.

Sweetflag Rhizome (Shichangpu)
[Treats] eye [disorders]. For a heart with pores [i.e., an absent or disturbed mind], take medicinal wine. Stops [the tendency to] forget much. Increases wisdom. Take sweetflag rhizome from afar, grind into fine powder. Every [dose] makes a person's ears and eyes sharp and bright. [Used] internally and externally.

translation:
[This passage is from the Internal Medicine section, discussing medicinal treatments for mental and neurological conditions. The following is a translation of the legible content:]

Yuan Zhi (Polygala root): Soak in water, decoct, remove the woody core, take the bark and flesh, decoct into a broth, have the patient drink it. Taking it as a powder with wine is also excellent.

Fu Shen (Poria with pine root): Promotes calmness, when taken it settles the spirit, nourishes essence, the flesh is used as the chief ingredient; taken as a powder with wine, it prevents confusion and is excellent.

Huang Lian (Coptis): Indicated for vexation, agitation, and restlessness. Used for nine spirits, also for fright and poor memory. Also good as a powder for treating cold-water conditions; taken together is especially excellent.

Shang Lu Hua (Phytolacca flower): For treating excess thought and brooding. The flowers are taken; dried in shade or as a powder with water, take one packet. Awakens the spirit effectively, take with water.

Chang Cao (Acorus): By custom this herb makes people joyful and cheerful; excellent for happiness.

He Huan (Mimosa/Albizia): In the courtyard it makes people joyful; within seven months it dispels sorrow and forgetfulness; its suffering is forgotten, sweetness remains.

Qiu Yin Si (Centipede silk): Used medicinally; decocted and given; helps the seven spirits; in seven months promotes health; removes forgetfulness; take regularly.

Lian Shi (Lotus seed): Calms the spirit; taken with ground mineral powder; taken long-term; ground into a thick gruel consumed regularly; brightens the complexion and reduces puffiness.

[General note]: Taken long-term, entering into meditative states; nourishes the flesh; taken regularly; brightens the complexion.

translation:
Magpie Head
Indicated for epilepsy and seizures. Take the flesh, roast it, and eat. Also, take two magpie heads and roast them; combine with one liang of red lead (dan), grind to powder, form into pills, and take. It may also be used in medicinal preparations. Per Han [formulary]: relieves prolonged suffering.

Bat (Fuyi / Vespertilio)
Indicated for epilepsy. Take a fresh bat, roast it whole, decoct and eat. It enters medicinal formulas. Bats remove vexation and calm the spirit. Roast and take in decoction. Good for calming fright and settling the mind. Per Han [formulary]: effective.

Musk (Guangxiang)
Indicated for epilepsy. True musk calms the will, settles the spirit, eliminates burning sensations. Take in decoction. Per Han [formulary]: effective.

Ox Gallstone (Niuhuang / Bezoar)
Indicated to supplement the heart, take blood into the extremities, good for various types of seizure and fright. Per Han [formulary]: effective.

Pig Heart
Indicated for fright and agitation; calms the heart and supplements the blood. For fright with sudden shock, loss of spirit, and fetal illness: steam it and eat. Six steamings. Effective for epilepsy and demonic qi. Per Han [formulary].

Zhenheche (Placenta)
This is the purple placenta (zihe che). Indicated for fear and terror, for those whose spirit has left the body. Governs epilepsy and mania, incoherent and excessive speech, inability to concentrate. Greatly able to calm the heart, nourish the blood, and quiet desires.

Ziheche (Purple River Cart / Human Placenta)
Steam until thoroughly cooked, use as a single preparation. Also effective externally.

Spirit [section]
Steam until cooked. Indicated for epilepsy. [Treatment methods follow.] Also treats the hundred yang conditions. For nocturnal episodes and recurrence of epilepsy, moxibustion at various points, three to seven cones, beginning from the tail [of the channel].

Acupuncture and Moxibustion Methods
[Needle the] Yongquan point below; [treat] the Yuyang [points]; if yin and yang are not communicating, and qi is not balanced and flowing freely, this can be harmful to the patient. Needling must follow these guidelines precisely in epilepsy.
